newsitem.title: CANADA: Hollinger not close to Fairfax decision.
newsitem.headline: Hollinger not close to Fairfax decision.

text.p: No decision is imminent on the fate of Conrad Black's stake in Australian newspaper group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd., the president of Black's Hollinger Inc. holding company said on Thursday.

David Radler said there was no rush to decide the future of the 25 percent stake in Australia's oldest newspaper group. Company executives, including Black, have often said they would shed the holding if they were prevented by government rules from boosting it to 50 percent.
The Australian government said Thursday it would not widen its media industry review to include foreign ownership.
"I knew that four weeks ago," Radler said in a telephone interview.

Black told shareholders at Fairfax's annual meeting that he had he had told Australia's Prime Minister John Howard Tuesday in their first meeting since Howard won election in March that he would like to raise his stake in the newspaper group.
Fairfax publishes the Melbourne Age, the Sydney Morning Herald and the Australian Financial Review newspapers.
Hollinger's newspaper interests include London's Daily and Sunday Telegraph, the Chicago Sun-Times, the Jerusalem Post, the Sydney Morning Herald and Southam Inc., Canada's biggest newspaper group.

Black said the Australian foreign media ownership rules, which bar foreign companies from holding more than 25 percent of newspaper groups and 15 percent of television companies, were "anachronistic".

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said Thursday he currently saw no need to change the foreign media ownership limits. Communications Minister Richard Alston said the government's current media review, originally designed to focus on cross-ownership restrictions, would not be broadened to include consideration of the foreign ownership rules.
Radler said that Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd. would be a motivated buyer of any Fairfax holding if cross-media ownership restrictions were lifted by the inquiry.

Packer, Australia's richest man, has a 15 percent stake in Fairfax through his media empire Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd., while fellow media baron Rupert Murdoch owns 5 percent of Fairfax through his News Corp media group.

Packer, because of his Australian Nine Network, is also prevented by cross-media ownership from raising his stake. He has said he would like to merge his company with Fairfax if cross-media ownership rules were relaxed.
